lessons.title: The dairy cow and her production cycle
lessons.html:
Understanding the lactation cycle

A dairy farm earns money from milk, and a cow only gives milk after she has calved. The supervisor must understand the cycle to plan feeding, breeding and milking. In South Africa the main dairy breeds are Holstein (Friesland), Jersey, Ayrshire and Guernsey, and many farms run crossbreds. Holsteins give high volumes; Jerseys give less milk with higher butterfat and protein.

The cycle

StageWhat happensManagement focus
Early lactationMilk rises to a peak; cow loses conditionHigh-energy feed, watch for ketosis and milk fever
Mid lactationMilk slowly drops; cow is bred againHeat detection, AI or bull, pregnancy test
Late lactationMilk falls further; cow regains conditionAvoid overfeeding, plan drying off
Dry periodNo milking, usually around two months before calvingDry-cow treatment as advised by vet, transition feeding

Most farms aim for one calf per cow per year, so the cow must be pregnant again within a few months of calving. Missed heats mean longer calving intervals and less milk per year.

Systems in South Africa

Pasture-based dairies, common in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and the Southern Cape, graze cows on irrigated kikuyu or ryegrass with a concentrate in the parlour. Total mixed ration (TMR) systems feed a mixed ration in feed lanes. Each system needs different daily routines, but the principles of good milking, feeding and health are the same.

lessons.title: Milking routine and milk hygiene
lessons.html:
A good milking routine

The milking routine affects milk quality, udder health and how much milk the cow lets down. Every milker must do it the same way at every milking.

  1. Bring cows in calmly. Shouting and hitting cause stress and poor let-down.
  2. Fore-strip a few squirts from each teat into a strip cup to check for clots or watery milk, which are signs of mastitis.
  3. Pre-dip or wash and dry the teats with a single-use paper towel per cow.
  4. Attach the cluster within about a minute of preparation, straight and without air leaks.
  5. Do not over-milk; remove cups when flow stops, or let automatic take-offs work.
  6. Post-dip every teat straight after milking to protect against infection.

Treated and sick cows

Cows treated with antibiotics must be clearly marked, for example with leg bands or spray, and milked last or into a separate bucket. Their milk must never go into the bulk tank until the withdrawal period on the label or from your vet has passed. One treated cow can contaminate a whole tank, and the buyer will reject it and charge penalties.

Cooling and cleaning

Milk must be cooled quickly in the bulk tank and kept cold until collection. Check the tank thermometer at every milking and record it. After each milking, clean the plant with the correct hot water and detergent cycle, and replace liners as the supplier advises. Milk buyers test for bacteria, somatic cells and residues, and pay on the results.

Safety in the parlour

Wet floors are slippery: wear gumboots with good grip. Cows can kick: never stand directly behind a cow. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling acid and alkali cleaners, and never mix chemicals.

lessons.title: Feeding, health and records in the dairy
lessons.html:
Feeding for milk

Milk is mostly water, so cows need clean water at all times; a high-producing cow can drink well over 100 litres a day. Feed must supply enough energy, protein, fibre and minerals. Feed the ration that the nutritionist or manager has set, and report when cows are not eating, when pasture runs short or when the TMR looks different.

Common health problems

  • Mastitis – udder infection; watch for clots, swelling and heat in the quarter.
  • Milk fever – low calcium around calving; cow cannot stand. Call the vet or follow the farm's treatment protocol.
  • Lameness – from wet, stony lanes or poor hoof care; it cuts milk and fertility.
  • Retained afterbirth and uterine infections – after calving.

Calf rearing

Every calf must receive good-quality colostrum soon after birth, ideally within the first few hours. Keep calf pens clean, dry and draught-free. Feed milk or milk replacer at the set times and in clean buckets, and offer calf starter and water early.

Records

Keep records for each cow: calving date, milk yields, heats, services, pregnancy results, treatments and drying-off dates. Use them to decide which cows to breed, dry off or cull. Records also prove that treated cows were withheld from the tank.

Key points

  • Plan work around the lactation cycle: calving, peak, breeding, drying off.
  • Follow the same hygienic milking routine at every milking.
  • Never put milk from treated cows into the bulk tank before the withdrawal period has passed.
  • Cool milk quickly and clean the plant after every milking.
  • Give calves colostrum early and keep good records for every cow.
